I downloaded the Garnett text myself (Project Gutenberg 1399, whose header reads Translator: Constance Garnett) and read the place in situ rather than trusting the verifier's line numbers. The sentence stands verbatim at line 7640: “Spring is the time of plans and projects. And, as he came out into the farmyard, Levin, like a tree in spring that knows not what form will be taken by the young shoots and twigs imprisoned in its swelling buds, hardly knew what undertakings he was going to begin upon now in the farm work that was so dear to him.” The chapter heading Chapter 13 is at line 7633 and PART TWO opens at line 5833 while PART THREE opens at 11868, so the locator Part Two, chapter 13 is right; the sentence opens the second paragraph, after Levin puts on his big boots and goes out to look after his farm. The preceding chapter closes “The real spring had come.”, which is the thaw the line answers. Translation drift checked in the only direction that matters here: the wording is Garnett's own, not a Maude or Pevear-Volokhonsky rendering blended in (Maude has “Spring is the time for making plans and resolutions”), so naming Garnett is not decorative. The 1901 date for Garnett's Anna Karenina (Heinemann) is standard and independently attested. shipped.js: not shipped, nothing near, Tolstoy 1 of 3 in the year (month 2), not banned; no second Tolstoy among April's 48 proposals or the 13 carry-ins, so the once-a-month rule holds. In scope: novel, 1877, translation 1901, no scripture, no lyric, nothing needing a warning. On theme, and gently so at six in the morning: it is the sentence a man says to himself when the ground has thawed.
